stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: In a three-year study of upland meadows, ecologist Moira Lindqvist compared plots heavily browsed by red deer with plots where browsing was light. Where deer were abundant, they stripped away the low shrubs that ground-nesting birds such as meadow pipits use to conceal their nests, and pipit nesting success fell sharply. Nuthatches and tits nesting in tree cavities at the plot edges, however, fared equally well under both conditions. Lindqvist's results suggest that fencing deer out of a heavily browsed meadow would most likely ______
choices: increase nesting success among ground-nesting birds but have little effect on cavity-nesting birds.
increase nesting success among cavity-nesting birds but have little effect on ground-nesting birds.
decrease nesting success among ground-nesting birds but have little effect on cavity-nesting birds.
increase nesting success among both ground-nesting birds and cavity-nesting birds.
explanation: Write the finding as an arrow: heavy browsing → shrubs lost → ground-nester success falls, while cavity nesters are unaffected. Fencing deer out reverses the condition, so the shrubs and their cover should return. The group that was harmed, ground nesters, should recover, and cavity nesters, who were never affected, should show little change.

B.why: You got the direction right but attached it to the wrong group. The passage says cavity nesters fared the same under both conditions. Ground nesters were the ones that depended on shrub cover.

C.why: You picked the right group but the wrong direction. Browsing lowered pipit success, so removing the browsing should raise it, not lower it further.

D.why: You assumed that what helps one group helps every group. Cavity nesters showed no response to browsing, so nothing in the passage supports a gain for them.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Many public health officials have assumed that a tax on sugary drinks reduces consumption about equally across a population. A study of one midsize city's two-cent-per-ounce soda tax complicates that view. After the tax took effect, soda purchases fell substantially in low-income households, for which the price increase was a noticeable share of grocery spending, but barely changed in high-income households. The study's findings suggest that if the city repealed the tax, ______
choices: purchases in high-income households would likely rise, while those in low-income households would change little.
purchases in low-income households would likely rise, while those in high-income households would change little.
purchases in low-income households would likely fall further, while those in high-income households would change little.
purchases in low-income and high-income households would likely rise by roughly similar amounts.
explanation: The finding: tax → purchases fall in low-income households, with little change in high-income ones. Repealing the tax removes the price increase. The group that responded, low-income households, would likely buy more again, and the group that barely responded would likely stay about the same.

A.why: You swapped the groups. High-income purchases barely moved when the tax arrived, so there is little reason to expect them to move when it leaves.

C.why: You kept the right group but missed that repeal reverses the change. Taking away the price increase should push purchases back up, not down.

D.why: You fell back on the popular view the passage sets up only to undercut. The study found the two groups responded very differently, so an equal response to repeal isn't supported.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Ceramic coatings are widely applied to turbine blades on the assumption that they reduce wear at any operating temperature. Materials engineer Tomas Okafor found otherwise. Above about 600°C, his coating fused into a hard, glassy layer, and coated blades wore far more slowly than uncoated ones. Below that temperature, the coating remained powdery, and coated and uncoated blades wore at the same rate. Okafor's results suggest that in an engine redesigned so that its blades run at 450°C instead of 700°C, ______
choices: coated blades would likely wear more slowly than uncoated blades.
coated and uncoated blades would likely wear at about the same rate.
coated blades would likely wear faster than uncoated blades.
coated blades would likely wear even more slowly than at 700°C.
explanation: The finding splits at 600°C. Above it, the coating forms a glassy layer and slows wear. Below it, the coating stays powdery and gives no advantage. At 450°C the redesigned engine is below the threshold, so coated and uncoated blades should wear at about the same rate.

A.why: You applied the high-temperature result to a low-temperature case. A wear advantage appears only above 600°C, and 450°C falls in the half of the finding where it disappears.

C.why: You overshot the change. Below 600°C the passage reports equal wear, not faster wear for coated blades. Losing an advantage is not the same as gaining a disadvantage.

D.why: You added an assumption the passage doesn't contain: that cooler running improves the coating's performance. The passage says that below 600°C the coating does nothing to reduce wear.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Many marine larvae drift for weeks before choosing a place to settle. Marine biologist Keiko Arashiro played underwater recordings in tanks and found that oyster larvae settled in far greater numbers near speakers broadcasting the crackling sounds of a healthy reef than near silent speakers. Mussel larvae, by contrast, settled at the same rate whether or not reef sounds were playing. Arashiro's findings suggest that if speakers playing healthy-reef recordings were installed on a degraded, quiet reef, ______
choices: mussel larvae would likely settle there in greater numbers, while oyster settlement would change little.
oyster larvae would likely settle there in smaller numbers, while mussel settlement would change little.
oyster larvae and mussel larvae would both likely settle there in noticeably greater numbers.
oyster larvae would likely settle there in greater numbers, while mussel settlement would change little.
explanation: The finding: reef sound → more oyster settlement, with no effect on mussels. Adding reef sound to a quiet reef applies that condition, so oyster settlement should rise and mussel settlement should stay about the same.

A.why: You attached the effect to the wrong species. Mussels settled at the same rate with or without sound. Oysters were the ones that responded.

B.why: You picked the right species but reversed the direction. Oysters were drawn toward reef sounds, so adding those sounds should increase their settlement, not reduce it.

C.why: You extended the oyster result to mussels. The passage says directly that mussel settlement didn't depend on sound.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Cartographers often add shaded relief (simulated shadows that make hills appear three-dimensional) on the assumption that it helps every reader judge terrain. A study by geographer Lena Fairweather tested that assumption. Novice map readers judged the relative elevation of points far more accurately on maps with shaded relief than on maps without it, whereas experienced readers, who infer elevation from contour lines, performed equally well on both. Fairweather's results suggest that removing the shaded relief from a hiking map would likely ______
choices: reduce experienced readers' accuracy in judging elevation while leaving novices' largely unchanged.
improve novice readers' accuracy in judging elevation while leaving experienced readers' largely unchanged.
reduce novice readers' accuracy in judging elevation while leaving experienced readers' largely unchanged.
reduce novice and experienced readers' accuracy in judging elevation by similar amounts.
explanation: The finding: shaded relief → better elevation judgments for novices, with no difference for experienced readers. Removing it takes away the aid, so novices should become less accurate. Experienced readers, who rely on contour lines, should be largely unaffected.

A.why: You swapped the groups. Experienced readers performed equally well with or without shading, so removing it shouldn't hurt them.

B.why: You picked the right group but the wrong direction. Novices did better with shading, so taking it away should lower their accuracy, not raise it.

D.why: You went back to the assumption the study was designed to test. The two groups responded differently, so an equal loss for both isn't supported.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Chloride from road salt seeps into concrete bridge decks and rusts the steel reinforcing bars inside. In a ten-year field study, civil engineer Rosa Delacroix found that heavy salting sharply accelerated rebar corrosion in decks made of ordinary concrete. In decks sealed with a waterproof membrane beneath the pavement, however, corrosion proceeded at the same slow rate seen in unsalted ordinary decks, whether the road above was salted or not. Delacroix's findings imply that where winter roads are heavily salted, a deck built with the membrane would likely ______
choices: corrode faster than an otherwise identical deck built without a membrane.
corrode at about the same rate as an otherwise identical deck without one.
corrode more slowly than an otherwise identical deck built without a membrane.
show no corrosion at all, unlike an otherwise identical deck without one.
explanation: Under heavy salting, the ordinary deck's corrosion is sharply accelerated, while the membrane deck stays at the slow, unsalted rate. Comparing the two under the same salted conditions, the membrane deck should corrode more slowly.

A.why: You swapped which deck is protected. Salt accelerated corrosion only in the ordinary decks, so the membrane deck is the slower one.

B.why: You ignored the condition the question names. The two decks corrode at similar rates only without salt. With heavy salting, the ordinary deck speeds up and the membrane deck doesn't.

D.why: You read 'no effect from salt' as 'no corrosion.' The passage says membrane decks still corroded, just at a slow rate.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: It is often claimed that eighteenth-century musicians simply favored slower tempos than modern performers do. Musicologist Anika Brandt argues instead that the room mattered. Comparing tempo markings that composers revised when works moved between venues, she found that in highly reverberant churches, fast passages were marked noticeably slower, probably so that rapid notes would not blur in the echo. Slow movements, however, kept their original markings. Brandt's findings suggest that if a lively dance movement written for a small salon were moved to a cathedral, it would likely ______
choices: be marked at a slower tempo, while a slow movement moved along with it would keep its marking.
keep its marking, while a slow movement moved along with it would be marked at a slower tempo.
be marked at a faster tempo, while a slow movement moved along with it would keep its marking.
be marked at a slower tempo, and a slow movement moved along with it would be slowed as well.
explanation: The finding: reverberant venue → fast passages marked slower, while slow movements stay unchanged. A lively dance moving into a cathedral meets exactly that condition, so it should be slowed. A slow movement on the same program would keep its marking.

B.why: You swapped which kind of movement changes. Brandt found that fast passages were slowed and slow movements were left alone.

C.why: You picked the right movement but the wrong direction. Echo blurs rapid notes, so composers slowed fast passages rather than speeding them up.

D.why: You extended the slowdown to every movement, which is the popular view Brandt argues against. The passage says slow movements kept their original markings.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Etchers have long dampened paper before printing, believing that moist paper picks up ink better from every part of a plate. Conservator Ilse Marchetti tested that practice. On dampened paper, ink transferred far more completely from deeply bitten lines than it did on dry paper, but shallow, lightly bitten lines printed equally well on both. Marchetti's results suggest that if an etcher who had always used dampened paper switched to dry paper, ______
choices: the shallow lines would likely print less fully, while the deep lines would print about as well as before.
the deep lines would likely print more fully, while the shallow lines would print about as well as before.
both the deep lines and the shallow lines would likely print noticeably less fully than before.
the deep lines would likely print less fully, while the shallow lines would print about as well as before.
explanation: The finding: dampening → fuller ink transfer from deep lines, with no difference for shallow lines. Switching to dry paper removes that benefit, so the deep lines should print less fully and the shallow lines should look about the same as before.

A.why: You swapped the line types. Shallow lines printed equally well on dry and damp paper. Only the deep lines depended on dampening.

B.why: You picked the right line type but the wrong direction. Dampening helped deep lines, so dropping it should make them print less fully, not more.

C.why: You accepted the traditional belief that the passage sets up to test. Marchetti found that shallow lines were unaffected by dampening, so they shouldn't get worse on dry paper.
